content.thinking:
I need to write this whole module in one pass without being able to typecheck, so I'm planning carefully using APIs I'm confident about. I'm designing a wizard's bookshelf prop group, thinking through whether it needs a root joint and how to structure parts without one if possible.

I'll keep it modest with three joints: a root, a hanging lantern, and a book flap that opens, plus a bookshelf roughly 2.2m tall with scrolls, candles, orbs, a rug, and a stack of floor books. I'm aiming for around 500 parts, merging small repeated geometry like books to stay efficient, and planning to use cel-shaded paints baked into an atlas for the toon style.

I'm weighing risk around merged geometry and painted UVs -- merging should preserve UVs so baking stays fine, so I'll trust the pipeline but hedge by reserving cel paints for larger surfaces like the wood frame and book covers, while keeping smaller props simpler.

Running the numbers for sixty books plus the shelf, total painted area lands around 10 m², so a 1024 paint size gives roughly 5mm texel density, which is plenty sharp. I could bump to 2048 for finer detail, but that pushes the atlas to 4096, which is heavier to render -- worth considering the tradeoff.

I'm also tracking my 64-flat-colour budget carefully: cel/paint colours don't count against that limit, so I'll rely on cel painting for the bulk of colour variation and save flat colours for just a few key uses, including any tinted textured parts. For the book spines, I'm planning around six shared SVG textures with gold bands and title glyphs, tinted per book rather than each needing a unique texture.

Each spine gets a thin transparent-background plane placed just in front of the cover, so only the gold ornament shows through over the painted cel colour beneath. I'm weighing whether to draw ornaments as grey-and-tint or directly in gold/cream/silver, leaning toward direct colour since that avoids extra tint variables, and I still need to work out whether these ~60 spine planes can be merged per texture into a single part rather than one per book.

Now I'm defining a book-building function that takes position, thickness, height, depth, and cover colour, constructing a cover box plus a slightly recessed pages box plus spine ridges, with the spine facing forward toward +Z so the plane geometry's default orientation lines up without extra rotation.

To cut the part count, I'll limit books to a handful of cover colours and merge geometry by colour group instead of per-book: 7 cel colours gives 7 merged cover parts (boards+spine combined per colour) plus one merged flat cream part for all pages, drastically reducing the total.

For this I need a bucketing system — a helper that builds box geometry at any position/rotation (so tilted books work via rotation matrices), then groups geometries by a bone+paint key using a Map, merges each group, and emits one part per bucket with its assigned fill. I'm still weighing how painted merged geometry interacts with per-part fill assignment.

I also need to check that mergeGeometries works across all the shape types I'm using (boxes, cylinders, spheres, cones, torus, lathe, plane) since they all share position/normal/uv attributes, while avoiding non-indexed geometry like ExtrudeGeometry. To keep merging safe I'll convert every geometry to non-indexed before combining, since mixing indexed and non-indexed breaks the merge — and for the faceted look I can just rely on low-segment spheres rather than manually recomputing flat normals.

Now I'm planning the actual scene dimensions: a centered bookshelf roughly 1.7m wide, 2.3m tall, 0.42m deep, done in a high-fantasy anime style with ornate gold trim, arched gothic crown, a crescent moon finial, twisting vine columns, and a deep midnight-blue/plum palette with teal magical glow and warm candlelight. I'm laying out the structure piece by piece — a stepped plinth base, side panels with fluted columns at the front corners — building up the geometry section by section.

Next I'm detailing the back panel as a starry indigo surface with gold decals for richness, then designing the shelf levels, including a lower cabinet with hinged doors (one slightly ajar) featuring brass handles and rune medallions, to add visual interest and joint complexity to the model.

Topping out at 2.40 for the last shelf tier, then the crown rises into a pointed arch to about 2.75 with a finial crescent, plus decorative items on top like an orb on a stand and candles. Total model height lands around 2.9 meters.

Now I'm working out the exact tier heights: boards at 0.72, 1.16, 1.60, 2.04, with the ceiling-facing top board sitting 2.46–2.52 before the gabled crown rises to 2.9, giving each tier roughly 0.40–0.42 of clearance. I'm also figuring the interior width—sides at ±0.80 with 0.05 thickness leave an inner span of about 1.55—and considering where to place vertical dividers between tiers.

Then I'm planning the carcass depth at 0.40 with the back panel near z=-0.19, leaving items room from -0.15 to 0.17 in z. For the first tier I'm laying out a leaning stack of books on the left, a glowing crystal ball on a brass tripod in the middle, and a cubby of scrolls on the right.

For the upper tiers I'm placing a trio of colored glass orbs on little stands, a stack of flat tomes topped with a candle, and maybe a small primitive owl figurine with glowing eyes for character. Higher up I'm adding an armillary sphere, an open grimoire on a lectern stand, and potion bottles to keep the wizardy theme, continuing with more books on the top tier.

For the bookshelf crown I'm topping it with a crown-and-orb finial, candles dripping wax, and a crescent moon, then working on the floor rug — using a flat circular textured plane layered over a thin cylinder base to fake a round woven rug sitting just above the floor.

I'm sketching the overall prop layout now: a round rug centered in front of the shelf, flanked by a stack of tomes with a candle and a wicker scroll basket on one side, and a tall iron candelabra stand on the other, keeping the whole footprint to roughly 1.3m wide and 1.5m deep as a cohesive prop group.

I considered adding a leaning library ladder for silhouette interest but decided it's too much extra work, opting instead for a hinged hanging brass lantern sign with a moon rune, mounted on a swinging bracket arm at height 1.9. I'm also noting the door hinge joints need to be set up for the left and right doors.

Now I'm carefully planning the imports, making sure only used modules are included to satisfy TypeScript's strictness, pulling in Three.js utilities, builder helpers, math and path functions, texture and toon-shading kits, and the paint mixing tools.

Picking a high-fantasy anime palette with cel-shaded indigo wood tones, lighter trim colors, and warm wood accents, reserving flat colors for glow effects and small details.

Still defining colors...

For each orb, I'll craft a texture with a vertical color gradient, swirling cloud patterns, and star-like sparkle dots, then layer small flattened white highlight spheres on top to simulate glossy anime-style specular reflections, giving each a distinct colored texture.

Now I'm sketching out the builder code: setting up joints, defining the root with default orientation, and planning stands for the orbs using lathe-based brass cup profiles with claw supports. Writing scene structure code...

Checking type exports to make sure Fill covers both string and Paint cases, deciding to just import Paint directly and define my own color type alias to avoid ambiguity.

I'm setting up a merge system: a map grouping geometries by color/material key, with helper functions to add geometries into buckets and flush them all into merged parts at the end, plus a placement helper that applies position and rotation transforms to a geometry via a matrix.

Adding box/cylinder/sphere builders...

I'm thinking through triangle budgets for the overall part count, making sure sphere segment counts stay low enough to keep the total under 60k triangles while still giving each piece distinct geometry.

Now I'm working out the shelf carcass layout, defining plinth tiers with specific widths, heights, and depths stacked at increasing y-positions to form the base of the cabinet.

Still writing geometry coordinates...

Adding gold ring accents at base/capital and a decorative spiral vine sweep winding around each column using a torus and helical sweep path.

To avoid ambiguity about which joint a sweep attaches to nearest, I'll explicitly assign `bone: root` to every sweep rather than relying on proximity. Then I add the back panel as a thin box behind the structure.

For the shelf area, I'm placing a single starry texture plane sized to span the visible tier region, centered appropriately and set slightly behind the shelf boards in z so it reads as a backdrop without poking through — the texture itself uses a deep indigo gradient with gold stars, crescent moons, constellation lines, and scattered dots, with items and shelf boards naturally occluding parts of it in front.

I'm now building each shelf board as a wood-grain box sized to fit between the side panels, adding a thin gold trim strip along the front edge, and considering small decorative touches like corbel brackets or a scalloped valance beneath each shelf for extra detail.

For the valance, I'll place a repeating row of small gold boxes rotated 45° like diamond teeth under the shelf edge, roughly 22 per shelf across all four shelves. Then I'm shaping the cabinet's top structure — a ceiling board, a cornice slab above the columns, and planning a gothic crown feature at the center.

I'm defining the pediment outline shape with ogee curves rising to a sharp peak, mirrored across the centerline, and extruding it to form the crown silhouette.

Adjacent cuts share edges so they stay under half, which is safe. For the crown geometry, I'm extruding the outline thin along the vertical axis and planning a slightly larger gold outline behind it as a trim border, offset backward to create a visible rim around the indigo crown.

Instead, I'll sweep a thin gold tube along the crown's outline path using a smooth curve through the profile points, positioned at the front face depth so it reads as a border highlight on the crown's edge.

For the crown's center emblem, I'm working out how to build a crescent moon shape by computing intersecting arc points between an outer and offset inner circle to carve out the crescent opening.

Working out the outer arc from +65° sweeping through 180° to -65°, then the inner arc closing back through the left side at angles near ±88.5° relative to the inner circle's center, forming the crescent outline before generalizing this into a reusable formula.

I'll write a `crescentOutline(s)` helper with no smoothing so the tips stay sharp, reusing it for the crown medallion, finial, and sign decoration. For the crown itself I'm planning a gold orb-and-spike finial on top plus small conical pinnacles at the crown's ends, sitting on the cornice shelf with the crown spanning the central width of the top.

I'm placing shelf-top decor in front of the thin crown piece — candles at a few x positions, a small orb on a stand, and a stack of tiny books with a candle — leaving the crown visible behind them. For the lower cabinet, I'm sizing and hinging the two front doors so each is about 0.76 wide by 0.50 tall, hinged at the outer edges of the cabinet opening.

Now I'm detailing one door: it's indigo with a raised inner panel bordered by gold trim strips, a glowing teal rune medallion in the center, a small brass ring handle near the seam, and brass cylinder hinges along the outer edge, all attached to a dedicated door bone rather than merged into the root mesh.

Adding a brass lock plate to the right door, then designing a book helper for shelf contents with parameters for tilt, thickness, and cover texture—building books at origin first so I can rotate them around their bottom corner before placing on the shelf.

Laying out book covers, spine, and pages...

Designing more spine variants...

Working out book dimensions with randomized thickness, height, and depth, positioning them front-aligned on the shelf with centers offset by half-depth, keeping heights capped for ceiling clearance, and cycling cover colors from a palette array.

For the end-of-row leaning book, I'm tilting it about 14° against its neighbor with the pivot at the bottom center. For horizontally lying books, I'm rotating the local axes 90° about z so the height direction maps onto x instead of y, keeping the spine face oriented toward the front.

I need to pin down the x-position so the book covers x ∈ [xRight - h, xRight], and figure out how the yaw rotation stacks with the 90° spine rotation given three's XYZ Euler order—rotating Z first, then Y, then X, so a small ry after rz=90 gives a believable messy tilt. For the bigger grimoires, I'll build a separate tome function with gold corner caps and clasps, plus a decal on the cover showing something like an eye or pentagram design.

Working out the clasp strap, glowing center gem, and the gold sigil decal texture on the cover, I'm computing the rotation needed to lay the cover plane flat facing up—rx=-90 makes +z point to +y—while also tracking how that rotation reorients the texture's "up" direction so the image still reads upright when viewed from above.

For the tome's physical form, I'm placing the spine on the viewer's left (-X side) with the top cover image's top edge toward -z so it reads correctly, then laying out local dimensions: cover width (x), depth (z), thickness (y), with top and bottom board boxes offset in y and a spine box connecting them.

Now I'm adding the inset pages box, gold corner caps at all four corners, a leather clasp strap with buckle across the fore edge, and a glowing center gem decal for the cover ornament. For scrolls, I'm planning horizontal parchment cylinders with darker inner cores, wrapped ribbon rings, and gold knob ends to cap each roll.

For the scroll rack cubby, I'm thinking of a pyramid arrangement of stacked scrolls (3-4-3) with their ends facing forward along the z-axis, so each scroll's spiral roll end is visible. I'll place small front-facing discs textured with a spiral pattern to mimic the rolled parchment look.

Now I'm working out the geometry: scrolls as cylinders rotated so their axis runs along z, hex-packed in rows (4-3-2) within a wooden cradle made of side plates and a bottom plate to hold them in place.

I'll add about nine scrolls total with ribbon color variants, plus a couple loose ones lying horizontal on another tier, and a dramatic unrolled scroll draping off a shelf edge as a textured plane with ragged alpha edges showing runic writing, topped by a rolled cylinder section at the top.

Now I'm placing an unfurled scroll hanging down from tier 1's shelf board over the compartment below, cream-colored with a torn wavy bottom edge and lines of rune text, visible only from the front. Then I'll move on to designing wax candle cylinders with varying radii.

I'll use LatheGeometry generally for flames, vase stands, orb stands, candle holders, and columns, building profiles that go from low to high y so normals face outward correctly, then give flames a warm amber glow color with a paler core.

For buckets I want an optional glow strength that gets applied via the glow function during flush, keeping it restricted to flat colors rather than painted materials. For candle holders and candelabras, I'll lathe a brass stem and saucer, then sweep individual arm curves topped with small lathed cups since sweeps can't be batched into buckets easily.

For candle drips, I'm planning thin cylinders with a sphere tip along the side plus a flattened wax pool at the base, with wax colors like cream, rose, pale teal, and lavender organized into bucketed cel-paint keys. Orbs will mostly be built as individual meshes since each has a different position and texture, with highlight details handled through a shared bucket.

For the highlight ellipsoids, I'm figuring out placement on each orb's upper-left-front surface using a normal direction offset from center, scaling a small flattened sphere into an ellipsoid shape, and orienting it so its local axis aligns with that surface normal using a quaternion rotation.

Let me simplify: rather than deriving a general rotation formula, I'll just pick simple Euler angle approximations for pointing the disc toward the highlight direction, like a small ry rotation combined with a small rx tilt, avoiding exact matrix derivation.

For the orb textures, I'm mapping u around the sphere and v pole to pole, with the seam at local −X so the front faces +Z at u=0.25; I'll draw a 256×128 texture with horizontal swirl bands, stars, and a vertical gradient from light at the bottom to dark at the top. For the stands, I'm using lathe-brass cups with claws holding the orb at a height based on stand height plus most of the radius, and considering adding a thin glowing torus ring around some orbs for a magical floating-aura effect.

An armillary sphere could work well on tier 3 — three gold tori at different angles orbiting a small glowing core on a base stand, kept simple with mostly non-glowing gold bands except the core. I'm also considering adding a couple of small potion flasks for charm, built cheaply as a lathe profile with glowing colored liquid, a cork, and a highlight rather than true glass transparency. For tier 3 I'm sketching an owl figurine perched to the right, building its body as a scaled ellipsoid in a violet tone.

I'm continuing the owl design: a lighter cream belly plane, a head sphere with cone ear tufts, glowing amber eyes with dark pupils, a gold cone beak, rotated ellipsoid wings, little cylinder feet, and a tail, perched elevated on a stack of books with each part assigned its own color bucket. I'm also working out a hanging sign on the left panel's outer side — an outward-sweeping bracket arm with a scroll curl, chains holding a signboard textured with a crescent and book icon.

Now I'm detailing the signboard itself: extruding a rounded rectangle outline painted indigo with beveled edges, adding a hinge joint at the arm tip so the sign can swing, and setting up textured decals on front and back faces (with the back rotated 180°), while sorting out the correct orientation so the artwork reads properly from the front.

For the top cover planes rotated -90, local +x stays world +x, so viewed from above-front the image appears upright with +x to the right. Now I'm sketching the rug as a flat painted cylinder sitting on the floor, with its pattern built from a base color plus additional details.

Adding fringe...

I'm placing the rug so it stretches from z=-0.2 to 1.7, slightly tucking under the shelf plinth's front edge since the rug thickness is negligible. Now I'm positioning floor props around it, starting with a stack of tomes off to the left beyond the shelf's width.

On the right side I'm adding a stack of five tomes topped with a candle and some dripped wax, and on the left a wicker scroll basket holding several tilted scrolls with ribbons, plus a tall three-candle candelabra nearby. I'm also considering a crystal ball on a carved wood tripod table near the rug's center as another floor piece.

Now I'm placing a glowing crystal orb on an ornate brass pedestal toward the front, with two tilted golden tori rings orbiting it for visual interest, deciding where it best fits in the composition relative to the shelf, book stack, and basket so nothing feels too cluttered.

I settle on putting the tome stack and candelabra on the viewer's left, and the scroll basket, crystal pedestal, and hanging sign on the viewer's right. Checking the overall footprint and height, I realize the crown's apex would push the total height too tall, so I scale down the crown height to keep the proportions reasonable for the tower setting.

Starting the implementation now, importing the builder, path, paint, and texture utilities I'll need...

Setting up the metadata block and palette colors, keeping the flat color count under the limit.

Now I'm defining the wood material with grain-based shading and a cel-paint helper that resolves lit colors into shadowed variants for the wood texture.

Shelf boards run with horizontal grain, side panels use vertical grain, and I'm setting up an indigo mottled paint for the frames, side panels, crown, columns, and doors to give it a hand-painted look. Still writing paint definitions...

Defining more color palette constants...

Still writing bucket logic...

Writing transform helper function...

Adding more primitive helpers...

I'm also planning book spine textures as small SVGs rendered onto a canvas, sizing stroke widths relative to the raster resolution so they stay visible.

Writing spine SVGs...

I'm planning five more spine designs (star, moon, vine, gem) with varied colors and band accents, then moving to the tome cover SVG with a gold border, flourishes, and a central sigil, considering a few color variants for the overall look.

For the remaining textures, I'm sketching a spiral-patterned scroll-end disc using parchment and dark spiral strokes generated via a loop, and then sizing out a starry background texture to fit the atlas dimensions.

Still designing textures... I'm laying out a sign texture with a book silhouette, crescent, and stars on a transparent backdrop, plus a circular rug texture with crimson fill, gold rings, and an eight-point star pattern in teal, gold, and cream.

Now I'm working through a door medallion with a glowing teal rune circle, a parchment scroll texture with ragged edges and rune squiggles plus a red wax seal, and starting a function for generating orb textures.

Still writing orb gradients...

Now I'm setting up shelf height constants and panel dimensions, then starting the carcass construction code for the plinth and side panels.

Writing plinth and trim geometry...

Adding gold frame strips and a diamond gem ornament to the side panels, then a back panel box in INDIGO_D, and starting on the shelf pieces using WOODH.

I realize those diamonds would overlap the door geometry at that depth, so I'll skip them on tier T0 and only add them for T1-T3. I'll also add vertical wood dividers between tiers 1-2 and tier 4, making sure placed items avoid those divider boxes.

Working out the top cornice and cap geometry...

Adding dentil molding under the cornice slab, then moving to position the side columns relative to the outer wall face.

Finishing the column lathe profile and adding gold torus rings at the top and bottom of each column, plus planning the capital finial using a spiral sweep for the vine.

I'll place four pinnacles at the corners near the base of the crown, then work out the crown's curved outline profile by defining a sequence of points that taper inward and upward from the wide base to a narrow peak, mirrored across the center for symmetry.

Mirroring the right-side points to build the left descending curve, closing the loop back near the starting corner, then typing the outline array as tuples of coordinates with smoothing flags for TypeScript.

Now I'm placing a crown band on the cornice with indigo color and slight bevel, then considering adding a gold crescent moon and star ornament embedded in the lower center of the crown.

Still placing crockets along the crown edge...

I'm adding a finial at the apex—a glowing teal orb sitting in a small gold cup—and realizing the crown is coming out too tall, so I'm scaling the whole profile down by 0.8 to bring the total height to around 3.2.

Now I'm moving on to the doors: setting up hinge joints for doorL and doorR on the body, then working out the geometry so each door spans roughly 0.77 units wide with a small gap between them, centering them symmetrically on either side with the hinge at the outer edge.

Still writing door panel and frame boxes...

Adding rivets and a glowing rune medallion plate to each door, then placing a ring-shaped handle and lock plate on the opposite door.

Behind the gap I'm adding a dark cabinet interior panel to hide the void, then moving on to carefully define each tier's contents with book and object placement ranges.

For tier one, I'm laying out a row of books on the left, a crystal orb on a tripod pedestal in the center, and a scroll rack segment, working out x-coordinate ranges for each so they fit within the shelf's clearance.

Then I'm adding a candle arrangement on the right—three stacked flat tomes topped with a candle holder and flame, checking the stack height plus candle and flame stay under the shelf above. Moving to tier two, I'm placing a wood divider and starting a taller row of books on the left side, then beginning to plan a set of three orbs on stands in the middle section.

I'm checking whether the hanging parchment at the shelf front overlaps the tier 1 candle stack, and considering moving it to the left side where books sit instead, though that would hide those contents too.

Trying hanging it over the cabinet doors instead: positioning it from T0 downward near the right door panel, offset to the right of the rune medallion so it doesn't fully obscure it, and widening it to 0.2 for readability while checking it still clears the medallion's extent.

For the parchment's actual geometry, I'm sizing it at 0.2×0.30 with a rolled cylinder top edge, then figuring out the z-depth so the plane sits in front of the door panel surface without clipping into the rune carvings -- settling on z=0.245 with the roll positioned just above the plane's top edge.

For tier 3 at height 1.60-2.00, I'm laying out a books row on the left, an armillary sphere with lathe-turned base and glowing rings in the middle, and an open grimoire resting on a small lectern stand on the right.

For the grimoire I'm building two cream page-blocks angled into a V shape with covers underneath, drawn page-line textures, plus tiny floating octahedron sparkles glowing teal above the book and a ribbon bookmark draping down the side. On the far right I'm placing an owl figurine perched on a stack of two tomes around x=0.58.

Moving to tier four, I'm laying out a row of books on the left, a three-candle candelabra centered around x=-0.10 kept under height limits, and a trio of tall potion flasks to the right, checking each item's height clears the shelf boundary above.

For the final tier, I'm adding horizontal tomes with a scroll resting on top, then adding orb and candle details on top of the shelf itself, spacing clusters like candles, tome stacks, and a small teal orb on a stand across the surface.

Now I'm setting up helper functions for generating books, defining a set of cover color palettes and a book function that takes position, dimensions, texture, rotation, and whether it's lying flat.

Still writing book geometry...

Writing row generation logic...

Still working out the leaning book rotation...

I'm setting a deterministic RNG seed for the row, adding a loop guard for max iterations, and checking tier clearances so leaning books don't overflow their slot height. Now I'm sketching the ornate "tome" function signature for a lying-down book with configurable dimensions and rotation.

For the tome geometry, I'm laying out the cover boards as thin top and bottom boxes, a spine box on one edge, and an inset pages block so the page edges peek out slightly from the covers. I'm positioning gold corner caps at the top cover's corners for the ornate detailing.

Still placing geometry...

Setting the cover's aspect ratio to roughly 0.26 by 0.34 so the texture fits well, sizing the decal plane to about 86% of the cover dimensions and rotating it flat against the surface. I'm also adding a small glowing teal gem sphere at the cover's center to give it a subtle relief highlight.

Now I'm defining the tome's overall transform, applying the cover color per bucket, and setting thickness around 0.05–0.07. I'm sketching out a scroll-building function next, laying parchment along the z-axis with end discs capped by spiral-textured poles.

Adding the ribbon wrap and seal...

Now I'm defining a horizontal scroll variant along the x-axis, with spiral-textured end caps facing opposite directions, a gold dowel running through the cylinder with capped ball ends, plus ribbon detailing — intended for loose scrolls on tier four and the tilted basket.

I realize I should generalize this into a single scroll function that builds pieces along the local y-axis by default, then composes a rotation transform to orient it along any arbitrary axis, working out the rotation math needed to reface the end caps correctly for each orientation.

Still defining scroll geometry...

Now I'm sketching out the candle function signature, planning the wax cylinder with its bucket-keyed color and thinking about whether to add a melt drip detail.

Adding an inner flame core with a brighter glow layered inside the outer teardrop shape, then moving on to designing the brass candlestick holder with a saucer base.

Still shaping the dish profile...the top disc stays flat with non-decreasing y values, and I'm adding a small brass torus handle standing upright on the rim. Now I'm moving to designing orb stands and clusters of candles, starting with a lathed brass profile for the stand's base shape.

Refining the cup profile with scaled radii and a gold torus ring at the rim, then placing the orb sphere itself with its own geometry, texture, and glow so it sits properly on top of the stand.

I'm making the orb's emissive texture fully bright for that anime glow effect, then adding white highlight ellipsoids positioned using a direction vector aimed toward the upper-right of the sphere's surface.

Working out the angle-of-orientation math for aligning the highlight ellipsoid with that direction vector, plus a smaller secondary highlight dot nearby.

Now I'm designing the hero crystal pedestal piece with orbiting rings, then moving on to an armillary sphere for tier three — building its lathe profile for the base and setting up the torus rings around it with their positions and tube radii.

I'm varying ring rotations for a tilted axis effect, adding a tilted rod through the center with small spheres and a glowing core sphere, plus a tiny moon detail attached to one ring. I'm checking the max height stays under 2.0, and deciding to skip a true tilt rotation in favor of varying each ring's rx angle instead, since composing an extra rotation per ring isn't straightforward with the current transform setup.

Now I'm starting the lectern geometry for the open grimoire on tier 3, building a lathe-profile pedestal stem positioned at the appropriate height.

Still working out page tilt angles...

I'll simplify by dropping the page tilt and just keeping flat pages with a texture plane around y=0.0215, since the tilt math was making the gutter edges intersect awkwardly. This whole local assembly then gets rotated by 22° about the book's pivot point.

For the page texture, I'm using a 60×100 viewBox with rune-like text strokes in dark brown over parchment background, applying the same texture to both pages since mirroring won't matter visually. The covers get a crimson leather color, and I'm adding a bookmark ribbon as a thin box positioned near the spine.

I'm scattering a few floating sparkle octahedrons and small glow motes around the lectern area at roughly y=1.90-1.95, checking they clear the plate top at y≈1.78. Next I'll move on to placing the owl figure on tier 3 of the lectern setup.

Now I'm building the owl piece by piece on top of the tome stack: starting with a tinted violet body ball at the base position, then adding a flatter belly ball layered slightly forward — defining offsets relative to a local origin before positioning the whole figure.

Still writing owl shapes...

Still adding owl details...

Checking the height math, owl on one tome stacks to about 1.945 against a ceiling near 2.0, so I'll shrink the hat and tilt it to fit. Now I'm moving on to designing the potion flasks for tier 4, starting with a lathe profile for the glass body.

Adding wax seal, parchment label, and highlight details to the flask, plus a small wooden tray stand for grouping them. Now sketching out the candelabra function signature for tier4 and floor placement.

Working out the arm geometry for the candelabra using torus arcs to form curved "U" shapes sprouting from the stem toward the cups, figuring out the angle and rotation needed to get the right orientation.

I'm reworking the arm geometry so it leaves the stem with a horizontal tangent and curves upward with a vertical tangent, trying different quarter-circle center placements to get that transition right.

For the right arm, I settle on a center above the stem point, mapping the arc as a -90° to 0° sweep of a torus segment to match the desired start and end tangents. Then for the left arm, I mirror this by using the 180° to 270° sweep instead, keeping the same center so both arms meet the stem symmetrically.

For a candelabra with more branches, I'm thinking through adding a second, taller pair of arms with a larger radius, making sure each arm's end height aligns with the top cup level by adjusting its starting height based on its own radius so all candle cups sit flush at the same height.

I'm also designing a more ornate central stem lathe profile with knobs and a ball mid-section, parameterized by overall height H, with the candle cups placed at the top of that stem.

I'm placing dishes on candelabra stems with varying candle heights for center and side positions, and checking that tier 4's clearance works out with stem height, cup placement, and flame height staying safely under the next tier's ceiling.

Now I'm moving to floor items, starting with a stack of five tomes near the base, varying their widths and depths with slight rotations for a natural stacked look.

I'm settling on a rug radius of 0.95 centered around z=0.9, placing the book stack off-rug on the bare floor at y=0, while the crystal pedestal sits on the rug itself with its base slightly raised to y=0.0125.

I'm checking distances for the candelabra and basket to confirm they clear the rug edge, moving the candelabra to x=-1.2, z=1.0 and verifying the basket and book stack both land safely outside the rug radius, while also making sure none of these floor items overlap the shelf's footprint.

Still building the basket geometry...

Working out the Euler angle math...

Now I'm designing a crystal pedestal hero prop with curled legs, a central lathed column, and a cup, sketching out the radial profile points for the lathe geometry.

Working out leg geometry...
